Comparison Technique
Identify points of similarity and difference in theme, form, language; PEEL paragraphs with cross-poem links.
Form
Genre and structure: sonnet, ballad, ode, free verse, dramatic monologue; choices signal expectations.
Imagery
Sensory pictures: visual, auditory, tactile; metaphor, simile, personification create meaning.
Sound Devices
Alliteration, assonance, sibilance, onomatopoeia, rhyme; create mood and emphasis.
Structure
Stanza arrangement, line length, volta in sonnet, enjambment, caesura; shape supports meaning.
Tone and Voice
Speaker's attitude (ironic, elegiac, defiant); persona may differ from poet; signalled by diction.
Banquo
Macbeth's friend whose descendants will be kings (witches' prophecy); ghost haunts banquet scene exposing Macbeth's guilt.
Divine Right of Kings
James I's belief monarchs chosen by God; murder of Duncan unleashes cosmic disorder (horses eat each other).
Hamartia: Ambition
Macbeth's 'vaulting ambition which o'erleaps itself' (1.7); drives murder of Duncan and tyrannical reign.
Lady Macbeth
Initially more ruthless than husband: 'unsex me here'; manipulates Macbeth's masculinity; descends into madness and suicide.
Three Witches
Weird Sisters open and propel plot; 'Fair is foul, and foul is fair'; embody supernatural and equivocation.
Tragic Hero
Macbeth is Aristotle's noble figure with fatal flaw (hamartia); ambition leads to downfall; arouses pity and fear.

Characterisation
The methods a writer uses to create and develop characters, through description, dialogue, actions and the responses of other characters.
Narrative voice
The perspective from which a story is told, such as first person ('I') or third person, which shapes how much the reader knows and how far they trust it.
Prose
Continuous written language in sentences and paragraphs, the form of novels and short stories, as opposed to the verse of poetry or the script of drama.
Setting
The time and place in which a story unfolds, which can create atmosphere, reflect themes and influence how characters behave.
Structure
The way a prose text is organised, including chapter order, time shifts, flashbacks and how tension is built and then resolved across the story.
Theme
A central idea or message explored through a text, such as love, power or identity, developed across the whole narrative rather than stated directly.

poetry-anthology-love-and-relationships-.d: Poetry Anthology: Love and Relationships / Conflict / Youth and Age
terms: Climbing My Grandfather (Waterhouse)
Andrew Waterhouse climbs grandfather like mountain; affection through physical detail and admiration.
Love's Philosophy (Shelley)
Percy Shelley; uses natural unity (fountains mingle with rivers) to seduce; 'why not I with thine?'
Mother Any Distance (Armitage)
Simon Armitage on moving out; mother holds 'one end of the spool'; love and independence stretched.
Porphyria's Lover (Browning)
Robert Browning dramatic monologue; lover strangles Porphyria with own hair to preserve perfect moment.
Sonnet 29 (Browning)
Elizabeth Barrett Browning; 'I think of thee' uses vine and tree imagery; love overwhelming and embracing.
Walking Away (Day-Lewis)
Cecil Day-Lewis on watching son leave; 'half-fledged thing'; love means letting go; parental ache.
